pack.description: Vocabulary of psychology passages and talks: cognition, learning, emotion and behavior.
pack.selection_note: Internal selection of terms that recur in introductory psychology texts; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: relating to the mental processes of thinking, learning and remembering
entries.example_academic: Sleep deprivation impairs a wide range of cognitive functions.
entries.example_spoken: Crosswords are supposed to keep your cognitive skills sharp.

entries.definition: the way people notice and understand things through the senses, or the way they think about something
entries.example_academic: Expectations strongly influence the perception of pain.
entries.example_spoken: There's a perception that the course is easy, but it isn't.

entries.definition: something that causes a reaction in a person, animal or plant
entries.example_academic: The infants looked longer at the unfamiliar stimulus than at the familiar one.
entries.example_spoken: Loud noise is a stimulus that most babies react to.

entries.definition: the process of training a person or animal to react in a certain way to a particular signal
entries.example_academic: Through conditioning, the dogs came to associate the sound with food.
entries.example_spoken: It's basic conditioning: the bell rings and everyone packs up.

entries.definition: something that makes a behavior more likely to happen again, such as a reward
entries.example_academic: Positive reinforcement proved more effective than punishment in shaping behavior.
entries.example_spoken: Kids respond better to positive reinforcement than to yelling.

entries.definition: a tendency to favor one view, person or result in an unfair way
entries.example_academic: Researchers used random assignment to reduce the risk of bias.
entries.example_spoken: I'll admit I have a bias toward morning classes.

entries.definition: describing thoughts and feelings that influence you although you are not aware of them
entries.example_academic: The advertisement was designed to appeal to subconscious desires.
entries.example_spoken: It was a subconscious decision; I didn't even think about it.

entries.definition: the ability to understand and share what another person is feeling
entries.example_academic: Reading fiction has been linked to higher levels of empathy.
entries.example_spoken: He has zero empathy for people who arrive late.

entries.definition: a sudden strong wish to do something without thinking about the results
entries.example_academic: Children who resisted the impulse to eat the treat performed better years later.
entries.example_spoken: I bought it on impulse and regretted it immediately.

entries.definition: a strong emotional bond with a person, especially between a child and the adult who cares for it
entries.example_academic: Secure attachment in infancy predicts healthier relationships in adulthood.
entries.example_spoken: She has a real attachment to that old bike.

entries.definition: the ability to recover quickly from difficulty or stress
entries.example_academic: Social support is one of the strongest predictors of resilience after trauma.
entries.example_spoken: It takes a lot of resilience to finish a PhD.

entries.definition: a deeply upsetting experience, or the lasting mental harm that it causes
entries.example_academic: Memories of trauma are often vivid but not always accurate.
entries.example_spoken: He's still dealing with the trauma of the accident.

entries.definition: a substance with no medical effect that is given to compare its results with those of a real treatment
entries.example_academic: Patients who received the placebo reported almost as much relief as those given the drug.
entries.example_spoken: Half the group got a placebo without knowing it.

entries.definition: to prevent something from happening or make it happen more slowly
entries.example_academic: Fear of criticism may inhibit participation in group discussions.
entries.example_spoken: Being recorded really inhibits me when I speak.

entries.definition: the ability to keep information in memory, or the act of keeping something
entries.example_academic: Spacing study sessions over several days improves long-term retention.
entries.example_spoken: My retention is terrible if I only read the slides.

entries.definition: a person's usual way of thinking about things
entries.example_academic: Students with a growth mindset interpret failure as information rather than as a verdict.
entries.example_spoken: You need a different mindset for oral exams.

entries.definition: a state of being alert, excited or physically ready to react
entries.example_academic: Performance on simple tasks improves as arousal increases, up to a point.
entries.example_spoken: A little stress raises your arousal and helps you focus.

entries.definition: a simple mental rule that people use to make a decision or judgment quickly
entries.example_academic: People rely on heuristics when they lack the time to analyze every option.
entries.example_spoken: My heuristic is: when in doubt, pick the longer answer.

entries.definition: most noticeable or important
entries.example_academic: Participants remembered the most salient details but forgot the context.
entries.example_spoken: The salient point is that the deadline hasn't changed.

entries.definition: the process of reacting less and less to something because it is repeated many times
entries.example_academic: Habituation explains why residents no longer notice the noise of passing trains.
entries.example_spoken: It's habituation: after a week you stop hearing the fan.

entries.definition: the uncomfortable feeling of holding two beliefs that do not fit together, or of acting against what you believe
entries.example_academic: To reduce cognitive dissonance, participants convinced themselves that the boring task had been enjoyable.
entries.example_spoken: That's cognitive dissonance: he hates the brand but keeps buying it.

entries.definition: the careful examination of your own thoughts and feelings
entries.example_academic: Early psychologists relied on introspection, a method later criticized as unreliable.
entries.example_spoken: After failing the exam, I did some serious introspection.

entries.definition: the effect by which seeing or hearing one thing influences how a person reacts to the next thing
entries.example_academic: Priming with words related to old age caused participants to walk more slowly.
entries.example_spoken: It's a priming effect: you see ads for pizza and suddenly you're hungry.

entries.definition: coming from outside a person or thing rather than from inside
entries.example_academic: Extrinsic rewards can reduce the pleasure people take in a task itself.
entries.example_spoken: Grades are an extrinsic reason to study.

entries.definition: belonging to the basic nature of a person or thing; coming from inside
entries.example_academic: Intrinsic motivation is associated with deeper and more durable learning.
entries.example_spoken: She has an intrinsic love of math; nobody pushes her.

entries.definition: the ability of the brain to change its structure and connections as a result of experience
entries.example_academic: Neuroplasticity allows undamaged regions to take over functions lost after a stroke.
entries.example_spoken: Thanks to neuroplasticity, adults can still learn languages.

entries.definition: awareness and understanding of your own thinking and learning
entries.example_academic: Training in metacognition helps students judge what they have not yet mastered.
entries.example_spoken: Metacognition is basically thinking about how you think.

entries.definition: the natural qualities of a person's character; a usual tendency to behave in a certain way
entries.example_academic: A cheerful disposition was associated with faster recovery from illness.
entries.example_spoken: He has a nervous disposition, so exams are hard for him.

entries.definition: the habit of thinking about the same worrying thing again and again
entries.example_academic: Rumination prolongs low mood by keeping attention fixed on the problem.
entries.example_spoken: Going for a run helps me break out of rumination.

entries.definition: the habit of noticing and trusting only the information that supports what you already believe
entries.example_academic: Confirmation bias leads investigators to overlook evidence that contradicts their first theory.
entries.example_spoken: That's confirmation bias: you only remember the times you were right.
